annotations.keyFindings: In 212 consecutive patients, a sit-to-stand count of 10 or fewer identified an anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min with sensitivity 78 percent and specificity 69 percent (area under the curve 0.77).
annotations.limitations: Cut-off chosen in the same data; testers unblinded for a third; 14 patients unable to complete testing excluded.

annotations.keyFindings: Reports sensitivity 71 percent and specificity 62 percent for gait speed below 1.0 m/s in 64 older patients.
annotations.limitations: No year, recruitment period, selection method or blinding reported.
annotations.notes: Not rated: the abstract lacks the information needed to judge relevance or method quality.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 15 studies, field-test sensitivity for a low anaerobic threshold ranged from 62 to 81 percent; no study validated a cut-off in a separate sample; patients unable to complete testing were usually excluded.
annotations.limitations: High risk of bias in included studies; heterogeneous tests.

annotations.keyFindings: A hospital combined both bedside tests for triage; exercise testing was done only after abnormal bedside results, so accuracy cannot be calculated.
annotations.limitations: Partial verification; no date; no numbers; rule chosen without description.
annotations.notes: Not rated: undated and without numbers; relevance and quality cannot be judged from what is reported.

annotations.keyFindings: Of patients prioritised by exercise testing, 46 percent started prehabilitation too late to complete four weeks because they waited for the test.
annotations.limitations: One centre; complications comparison confounded by fitness.

annotations.keyFindings: Of 1,120 referred patients, 9 percent could not complete exercise testing; they had the most complications; excluding them overstates specificity.

Estimating a sensitivity of 80 percent within 10 points needs about 62 patients with the target condition, about 155 in total at 40 percent prevalence; cut-offs chosen in the same data inflate accuracy.
annotations.limitations: Methods guidance, not empirical accuracy data.

claims.text: In 212 consecutive patients awaiting major abdominal surgery, a sit-to-stand count of 10 or fewer identified an anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min with sensitivity 78 percent and specificity 69 percent.
claims.passage: A count of 10 or fewer identified an anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min with sensitivity 78 percent and specificity 69 percent.
claims.interpretation: Pre-specify 10 or fewer as the cut-off to validate; the published accuracy is probably optimistic.

claims.text: Across 15 accuracy studies of field tests against exercise testing, no study validated a cut-off in a separate sample.
claims.passage: no study validated a cut-off in a separate sample
claims.interpretation: The local study should validate pre-specified cut-offs, not derive new ones.

claims.text: Of 1,120 patients referred for exercise testing before major surgery, 9 percent could not complete a test, and excluding them overstates specificity.
claims.passage: Of 1,120 patients referred for exercise testing before major surgery, 9 percent could not complete a test
claims.interpretation: Classify inability to complete testing by a pre-specified rule rather than excluding those patients.

claims.interpretation: With about 40 percent prevalence, recruit about 155 plus those without a usable reference result.

claims.text: An undated conference abstract reported sensitivity 71 percent and specificity 62 percent for gait speed below 1.0 m/s in 64 older patients.
claims.passage: Gait speed below 1.0 m/s identified an anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min with sensitivity 71 percent and specificity 62 percent.
claims.interpretation: A candidate cut-off for gait speed, from an unrated source that cannot be appraised.

claims.text: Of patients prioritised for prehabilitation by exercise testing at one centre, 46 percent started too late to complete four weeks because they waited for the test.
claims.passage: 46 percent started prehabilitation too late to complete four weeks before surgery because they waited for the test
claims.interpretation: Speed of triage matters; a bedside test only helps if it is accurate enough.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; two undated grey records are left unrated. One study found a sit-to-stand cut-off of 10 or fewer detected a low anaerobic threshold with sensitivity 78 and specificity 69 percent, but chose the cut-off in its own data. A review found field-test sensitivity of 62 to 81 percent, no validated cut-off and routine exclusion of patients who cannot complete exercise testing, which overstates specificity. Waiting for exercise testing delayed prehabilitation for almost half of prioritised patients elsewhere. The evidence supports a validation study of pre-specified cut-offs in consecutive patients, not a switch to bedside triage now.
gradeRationale: Single-centre accuracy studies with cut-offs derived in the same data, a review of studies at high risk of bias, and unappraisable grey reports; serious risk of bias and imprecision.
summary: Seven records appraised; two undated records left unrated with null scores; six claims.
